https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/mag.text: The Budapest Times Magyar urges patience as government marks five months in office At the first stop of his autumn tour of the country, on Saturday in Veszprém, Péter Magyar also spoke about the significant expectations and hopes directed at Tisza regarding the restoration of order in the country and accountability, indicating that many results have already been achieved, but that a rule of law can only be rebuilt and operated by rule-of-law methods. The Prime Minister and president of the Tisza Party opened his speech by noting that many people had told him the party should focus on governing rather than touring the country — passing legislation, building up the bottom threshold, bringing home EU funds, and getting the economy going — but that in his view, going among the people is very important. “What has set Tisza apart from the political elite of the past, from the very beginning, is that it does not envision politics, shaping public life, or professional proposals without the people, but together with them,” he said. He added that the fruits of this work had ripened five months ago, and that this was “something we really shouldn’t stop.” Péter Magyar said he is grateful to local communities for the fact that, after smaller and larger periods of rest and reorganisation, more and more people are once again becoming active in the Tisza Islands. This is indicated, he said, by the fact that around a thousand people applied for the positions of county coordinator and national president of the Islands by the 10 September deadline. He added that the next task is for the Tisza presidency to review these applications and select the most suitable candidates, after which the Island members will decide on the individuals to serve as regional presidents and national president. The prime minister recalled that Tisza has been governing for five months, during which time he has had to travel abroad frequently and foreign leaders have also visited Hungary. As he put it, everywhere they see that there has been “a huge, elemental, truly earth-shattering change” in Hungary, and people’s trust is not waning but rather growing, with more and more people coming to understand that this was a necessary change. According to the prime minister, success requires hard work, honesty, and humanity. He also touched on the fact that mistakes can be made, but one must learn from them. “We are on the right path toward joining hands with one another,” declared Péter Magyar. The prime minister pointed out that the closing of an era does not mean that those who have committed crimes should not face punishment, nor that stolen assets should not be recovered. But ordinary Hungarian citizens must genuinely extend a hand to one another and must be able to have conversations again, stressed Péter Magyar, thanking those supporters of Tisza and Fidesz who have already done so. To the “propagandists,” he sent the message: keep working, stand by your principles, “it can be done without public funds too.” If someone is a good journalist, if someone is a “talented propagandist,” there will be demand for them, people will read and watch them — “as long as they are not stealing hundreds of millions in the process, and not doing so with Hungarian people’s money,” he said. The prime minister recalled several moments from the campaign and the election night victory of 12 April, then stated that the nationwide tour is not about continuously campaigning and trying to persuade people, but about the fact that the energy and momentum have been maintained. He added that they are striving to meet expectations, but will not be able to satisfy everyone as a government. “We must look after the interests of all of Hungary and every Hungarian person,” he said, pointing out that they had committed to being the government of every Hungarian. The state treasury has been, or still is, hollowed out to such a degree, he continued, that had it not been for the positive market expectations generated by the elections and Tisza’s programme, the country could have faced insolvency as early as the end of April. The prime minister added that, thanks to the well-founded programme and credible professionals, investors believed that Tisza would be able to bring home EU funds and curb the budget deficit; as a result, bond yields and the cost of financing Hungary’s national debt fell radically, and no payment problems emerged. He stressed that there is “an extraordinary level of expectation and extraordinary hope” directed at Tisza and the ministers — including Finance Minister András Kármán — from the budget and every sphere of society, and that this is a demanding task. As he said: he is proud of his party’s 240-page, four-year programme; they are trying to deliver as much of it as possible, but that does not mean every commitment will be fulfilled within two or three months, which is why he is asking everyone for their patience, understanding, and trust. In his assessment, what is taking place is not Facebook governance — it is very important that people hear about results, mistakes, and failures first-hand, or, for example, hear a prime minister apologise when he acknowledges that he was wrong or failed to listen to someone. It may sometimes be a lot, but following Péter Magyar’s Facebook page and watching every video is not compulsory — “sometimes even I get bored of myself.” It is important to keep people informed; not everything can always be understood from just two words, he explained, justifying his activity. He touched on the establishment of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) and the nomination of five constitutional judges, among them Miklós Ligeti, whom many had expected to head the NVVH. Péter Magyar said that when he spoke with Miklós Ligeti about his nomination as a constitutional judge — which represents the pinnacle of the legal profession — he did not get the impression that Ligeti felt he had been sidelined. Regarding the Road to Prison program, the prime minister emphasized that they would provide every assistance to the investigating authorities, “freeing them up,” and that not only the national police chief but also the county chief constables had been replaced. He listed further steps: the new president of the republic would soon propose a chief prosecutor, parliament would elect that person by the end of September, the prosecutor’s office would also “start functioning,” and the tax authority had a new head who had been selected through an open competition. The rule of law can only be rebuilt and operated by rule-of-law means, declared Péter Magyar, adding that many people feel the urge “to hear the handcuffs click,” but that is not how it works. “Even in films, the first ten minutes aren’t always the most exciting or the best — there will be much more to come that we may not even be able to imagine right now; the authorities will be at work,” the prime minister promised. He elaborated that the government was proud of its measures to date, including doubling the social firewood allowance, making prescription medicines VAT-exempt, and working on wage adjustments in the social sector, child protection, healthcare, law enforcement, and education. He said that before 12 April, the former prime minister had passed judgment “with his cronies and janissaries” on the Hungarian people, declaring who could get what and what opportunities they could access, but at the election, the Hungarian people passed a perfectly clear judgment on them. He noted that Tisza cannot tolerate these people “lying to people’s faces” in parliament, which is why “we’d rather laugh at them, because that bothers them more.” Péter Magyar asked the Tisza community to be open and welcoming. He said that sometimes those who want to join after the fact can seem suspicious, but there are people with very good intentions who could not afford to voice their opinions under the previous system. The trust of those who are doubtful or rooting against us must be built up, he stressed, noting that it must be explained to them that Tisza is working for the whole country, so that things will be better for everyone. Speaking about the 23 October anniversary celebrations marking the 70th anniversary, he emphasised that this will be a “tremendous event,” people will come from all over the world, a great many eyes will be on Hungary, and this event had to be organised with virtually no money in the treasury. Speaking about the rise in diesel prices, he said the cabinet is doing everything it can to mitigate the effects, but a price cap is not an option at this moment, as it would cost the Hungarian budget 50–100 billion forints per month. At the end of his speech, Péter Magyar drew his audience’s attention to the fact that a liveable, functioning and humane Hungary requires everyone, then thanked the islands and the activists for their work and support over the past two and a half years. https://aa.com.tr/en/russia-ukraine-war/.text: Russia-Ukraine War Zelenskyy says Ukraine did not receive early warning from partners on overnight strikes in Kyiv President claims Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries for 2 days Burc Eruygur 13 October 2026 • Update : 13 October 2026 ISTANBUL Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that his country did not receive an early warning from its partners on overnight Russian strikes on the capital Kyiv. In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy claimed that over 100 different weapons were used in overnight strikes by Russia, including ballistic missiles, hitting civilian infrastructure. “Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said. Commenting on an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv announced by US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy said Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or on the country’s energy sector in general for the two days since the announcement. “But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” Zelenskyy added. He said Ukraine’s readiness for “reciprocal steps toward de-escalation” has not changed, arguing “effective” pressure on Russia is needed for de-escalation, and that wars end “when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war.” “Global pressure on Russia contributes to exactly that – bringing peace closer. But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed,” he added. The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a separate Telegram statement that one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the capital’s Darnytskyi district, as Ukraine claimed downing 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight. In a statement, the country’s Air Force added that Moscow launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles against Ukraine from the Russian border region of Bryansk. Separately, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told a panel of the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland that Kyiv continues to receive intelligence data from the US. “Yes, we continue this cooperation (with the American side). And, also, it is true that yesterday’s attack, or night attack, (the) air raid alert was launched with a delay. But it is because of (the) special type of the weaponry which was used by (the) Russian side,” Sybiha said.
